laws.title: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015
laws.replaces: Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinance, 1968, in its application to Sindh (s.14).
laws.scope: Industrial and commercial establishments in Sindh employing 10 or more workers (now, or on any day in the previous 12 months), plus classes notified by Government. Not applicable where government statutory service rules apply. Some Standing Orders (e.g. SO 13 bonus, SO 15 closure) do not initially apply to industrial establishments with 20 or fewer persons.

amendments.title: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) (Amendment) Act, 2021
amendments.summary: Adds 'seasonal worker' as a class with a seasonal card (SO 1(a)(vii), SO 1(h), SO 2(7)); removes the old proviso in SO 16(6) that gave seasonal workers one month's gratuity per season; inserts SO 20-A (extra month's wages at the end of a season).

key_provisions.point: Applies to industrial and commercial establishments with 10 or more workers.
'Worker' includes permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, apprentice and contract workers, but not an occupier or manager who has hiring and firing authority.
The employer must display the Act in English, Urdu and Sindhi (and in the language of the majority of workers) near the entrance and in all departments.
Contravening the Standing Orders is punishable with fines; prosecutions are brought by the Inspector and tried by the Labour Court.
No discrimination on the basis of gender, religion, political affiliation, sect, colour, caste, creed or ethnic background in enforcing the Act.

Classes of worker: permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, apprentice, contract worker (seasonal worker added in 2021). Probation is 3 months; a worker engaged on work likely to last more than 9 months becomes permanent after satisfactorily completing 3 months' probation. Temporary work is work likely to finish within 9 months.
Every worker must be given an appointment letter at the time of appointment stating the terms and conditions of employment, including wages. Transfers and promotions must also be given in writing.

Paid holidays and leave apply as provided by law; all festival holidays declared by Government are paid. A leave application must be decided within a week, and a refusal must be recorded in writing with reasons.
Wages must be paid before the 7th day after the wage period ends (establishments with up to 1,000 workers) or before the 10th day (more than 1,000 workers).
In commercial establishments, work beyond 9 hours a day or 48 hours a week must be paid at twice the normal wage rate.

Establishments with 20 or more workers must insure all permanent workers (group insurance) against natural death, disability, and death or injury not covered by workmen's compensation or social security law; if the employer fails, the employer pays the equivalent amount.
Workers laid off because of plant failure, curtailment of production or similar causes get half their daily wages as compensation for the first 14 days of lay-off.

An employer may not terminate more than 50% of the workers or close the whole establishment without prior Government permission (except for fire, catastrophe, power stoppage, epidemic or civil commotion).

Terminating a permanent worker for any reason other than misconduct requires one month's notice, or one month's wages (average of the last 3 months) in lieu. The same one-month notice applies when a permanent worker leaves.
Temporary workers, probationers, badlis and contract workers are not entitled to notice of termination (and need not give notice when leaving).

No worker may be terminated, removed, retrenched, discharged or dismissed except by a written order that explicitly states the reason. An aggrieved worker can use the individual grievance procedure of the Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013.
key_provisions.note: The Standing Order cross-refers to 'section 37' of the Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013; the grievance section of that Act is s.34, and High Court of Sindh judgments apply s.34 together with SO 16(3).

key_provisions.point: On termination, earned wages and other dues (including payment for unavailed leave) must be paid before the end of the second working day.

On resignation, or on termination for any reason other than misconduct, the worker gets gratuity of one month's wages for every completed year of service (or part of a year above 6 months) - unless, for that period, the employer ran a provident fund with an employer contribution at least equal to the worker's (and the provident fund amount is not less than the gratuity).
key_provisions.note: Wording as amended by Sindh Act No. XXVIII of 2021 (seasonal-worker proviso removed).

key_provisions.point: A worker is entitled to the full provident fund balance, including the employer's contributions, even after resigning or being dismissed.

If a worker is not allowed to work or to mark attendance, the worker may report this in writing to the area Inspector within 10 days; the employer is then barred from initiating action against the worker.
A permanent worker is entitled to a service certificate when the employment ends for any reason.
Retrenchment within a category is last-come, first-go; retrenched workers get preference if the employer hires again within one year.
A seasonal worker who worked throughout the season (at least 75% of its days) gets one extra month's wages at the end of the season.

Misconduct includes wilful insubordination, theft, fraud or dishonesty, wilful damage, bribery, habitual absence or absence without leave for more than 10 days, habitual late attendance, riotous behaviour, habitual negligence, illegal strike and go-slow.

No dismissal for misconduct unless the worker is informed in writing of the alleged misconduct within one month and given a chance to explain; an independent inquiry is required and the worker may nominate a co-worker to assist.
Suspension pending inquiry may not exceed one week at a time or four weeks in total (with limited exceptions), and full wages are payable during suspension.
A worker occupying employer-provided housing must vacate it within 2 months after the employment ends; after that the employer may seek summary eviction from a First Class Magistrate.

caveats: Applies only where 10 or more workers are employed - confirm the size of the establishment first.
If the employer operates in more than one province (trans-provincial), federal law and the NIRC may apply instead of Sindh forums - see federal-industrial-relations-2012.

laws.title: Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015
laws.replaces: Payment of Wages Act, 1936, in its application to Sindh (s.29).
laws.scope: Persons employed in factories, industrial and commercial establishments, mines and railways in Sindh.

key_provisions.point: Covers commercial establishments including banks, insurance companies, clubs, hotels, restaurants, departmental stores, cinemas, schools, colleges and private educational institutions, hospitals, private health centres and clinical laboratories, and private security agencies run on a commercial basis.
'Employed person' includes permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, apprentice and contract workers, but not an occupier or manager with hiring and firing authority.
Every employer, including a contractor, is responsible for paying the wages of persons employed by them.
The employer fixes wage periods; no wage period may exceed one month.
Wages must be paid before the 7th day after the wage period (where fewer than 1,000 persons are employed) or before the 10th day (others), on a working day.
When the employer terminates employment, earned wages must be paid before the end of the second working day.
Wages must be paid through a crossed cheque or bank transfer, together with a pay slip showing the details.

Only listed deductions are allowed: fines, absence, damage or loss caused by the worker's neglect, approved amenities or services, recovery of advances or overpayments, income tax, court orders, provident fund, and approved co-operative or insurance payments.

Fines only for acts or omissions approved and displayed in a notice, and only after a chance to show cause; total fines in one wage period cannot exceed 3% of wages, and cannot be recovered in instalments or after 60 days.

Claims about illegal deductions, delayed wages, or unpaid provident fund or gratuity dues are decided by an Authority notified for the area (a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation or a Directorate of Labour officer of at least grade 18).

The worker, a lawyer, an authorised trade union official, a Labour Inspector or the worker's heirs may apply, within 3 years of the deduction or of the date the wages were due (later only if sufficient cause is shown).

The Authority can order refund or payment plus compensation of up to 10 times the amount deducted (no compensation for delay caused by a bona fide error or dispute, an emergency, or the worker's failure to collect).
A malicious or vexatious applicant can be ordered to pay the employer a penalty of up to Rs 5,000.
One application can cover a group of workers of the same establishment whose wages for the same period are unpaid; in a group application compensation is capped at Rs 10 per worker.
Appeal against the Authority's direction lies to the Labour Court within 30 days (an employer must first deposit the amount ordered).
Discrimination in wages between men and women is punishable with a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000 (Rs 50,000 to 75,000 for a repeat offence).
Any contract or agreement by which a worker gives up rights under this Act is void to that extent.
On closure, insolvency, winding up or liquidation, workers' dues (wages, gratuity, provident fund) are recovered from the proceeds.
No discrimination on grounds of sex, religion, descent, tribe, political affiliation, sect, colour, caste, creed or ethnic background in enforcing the Act.

caveats: The Authority for each area is notified by Government; the Sindh Labour Department can say which office handles a given district.
A separate 6-month claim route exists for minimum-wage shortfalls (see sindh-minimum-wages-2015, s.10).

laws.title: Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015
laws.replaces: Minimum Wages Ordinance, 1961; Minimum Wages for Unskilled Workers Ordinance, 1969; Employees Cost of Living Allowance (Relief) Act, 1973 - in Sindh (s.21).
laws.scope: All industrial and commercial establishments in Sindh.

amendments.title: Sindh Minimum Wages (Amendment) Act, 2018
amendments.summary: Mentioned in a High Court of Sindh judgment; text not yet reviewed.

key_provisions.point: Applies to all industrial establishments and commercial establishments in Sindh.
An adolescent is a person aged 14 to under 18; an adult is 18 or older.

'Commercial establishment' includes banks, insurance companies, clubs, hotels, restaurants, cinemas, schools, colleges, private educational institutions, hospitals, private health centres, laboratories and private security agencies run on a commercial basis; the Act also applies to employees of registered societies and voluntary social welfare organisations.
Minimum wages include basic pay plus statutory allowances (cost of living allowance, dearness allowance and ad hoc relief).
'Worker' excludes Federal and Provincial Government employees and persons employed in an employer capacity or notified as occupier/manager.
Minimum rates are recommended by the Minimum Wages Board and declared by Government notification in the official Gazette; they take effect on publication unless another date is given.
No employer may pay a worker less than the declared minimum rate (subject only to authorised deductions).
Workers already entitled to higher wages under an agreement, contract, award or custom keep the higher wages.
Paying below the minimum rate is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000, or both - plus paying the worker the shortfall.

An Authority notified for the area hears claims for non-payment or delayed payment of minimum wages; the worker (or someone authorised) applies within 6 months of the due date (up to 1 year with sufficient cause); the Authority can order payment plus a penalty of up to 10 times the wages withheld.
Appeal against the Authority's order lies to the Labour Court within 30 days.
Factory and shop inspectors are also inspectors under this Act (shop inspectors for shops and establishments with 9 or fewer workers).
Discriminating between men and women in paying minimum wages is punishable with a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000 (Rs 50,000 to 75,000 for a repeat offence).
No discrimination on the basis of sex, religion, political affiliation, sect, colour, caste, creed or ethnic background in enforcing the Act.

caveats: Never hardcode the rate - read the current figure from current_rates.json.
The 2018 amendment has not been reviewed yet.

laws.title: Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013
laws.scope: Persons employed in any establishment or industry in Sindh, including fishing and agriculture, with listed exclusions.

key_provisions.point: Applies to persons employed in any establishment or industry in Sindh, including fishing and agriculture; excludes, among others, police and defence services, State administration (other than Railway and Pakistan Post workmen), certain security and fire staff, and non-commercial hospitals/care institutions and non-commercial education or emergency services.
Workers may form and join trade unions of their choice without prior authorisation; where women are employed, the union executive must include women in proportion to their employment.

Unfair labour practices by employers include refusing to employ, discriminating against, or dismissing, transferring or threatening a worker for being a union member or office-bearer or for union activity.

A worker can bring a grievance about any right under any law, award or settlement to the employer's notice in writing (personally, or through the shop steward or collective bargaining agent) within 3 months of the day the cause arose.
The employer must communicate a written decision within 15 days (within 7 days if the grievance was raised through the shop steward or collective bargaining agent).
When the matter is taken to the Labour Court, it must decide within 90 days.
If the employer does not decide in time, or the worker is dissatisfied, the worker may take the matter to the Labour Court within 60 days of the employer's decision or of the end of the reply period.

Not complying with a Labour Court decision under s.34 within 7 days (or the time set) is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months, or fine up to Rs 500,000, or both (prosecution on the worker's written complaint).
Workers with a common grievance arising from a common cause may file a joint application.
Labour Courts are presided over by a serving or former District Judge or Additional District Judge.
No court fee is payable for filing documents in a Labour Court.
An appeal against a Labour Court's final decision (including under s.34) lies to the Labour Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of communication of the decision.
A worker may be represented by an office-bearer of the collective bargaining agent; lawyers may appear before the Labour Court or Tribunal with its permission, but not in conciliation proceedings.

caveats: Text checked against the High Court of Sindh Judges' Library compilation (September 2014); later amendments and the Sindh Industrial Relations Rules, 2021 have not been reviewed.
Trans-provincial establishments may fall under the federal Industrial Relations Act, 2012 (see federal-industrial-relations-2012).

laws.title: Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025
laws.scope: Domestic work in or for households across Sindh (child care, elderly care, sick care, natal/post-natal care and ancillary work).

key_provisions.point: Extends to the whole of Sindh and came into force at once. The published s.1(1) calls it the 'Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Bill, 2025' (a drafting slip; the notification publishes it as an Act).
No child below 16 may work in a household in any capacity; workers under 18 may only do light work that does not harm health or development.

Harassment complaints by a woman domestic worker against a household or employer (or by female household members against a domestic worker) fall under the Ombudsperson appointed under s.7 of the 2010 workplace harassment law.

No bonded or forced labour; no discrimination (religion, race, caste, creed, sex, ethnicity, place of birth, domicile, migration, etc.); the worker must be addressed as a 'domestic worker', not a 'servant'; no extra work without free consent and extra pay; dignified working conditions and safety; benefits include social security and old-age benefits.

Every domestic worker must be given a letter of employment in the prescribed form, with a copy sent to the Inspector (manually or digitally); existing workers were to receive letters within 60 days of the Act's commencement.
Full-time and live-in workers work only 8 hours a day; no domestic worker may be required to work more than 6 days a week (a 7th day only by mutual agreement, at double wages).

Festival holidays with full pay according to faith; 6 weeks' paid maternity leave (paid directly by the employer if the worker is not registered with an institution); 10 casual leaves (at most 2 consecutive days) and 8 sick leaves (with a medical certificate) per year on full pay.
Wages may not be less than the minimum wage notified under the Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015.
Live-in workers who choose to live at the workplace must get adequate accommodation and decent living conditions.
A yearly medical examination and prescribed vaccinations at the employer's cost.
Termination requires one month's written notice by either side, or one month's wages (average of the last 3 months) in lieu.
Wages are due within 5 days after the wage period (which cannot exceed one month); when the employer terminates, earned wages must be paid within 2 working days; payment in coin or currency notes.

Paying below the minimum wage: fine up to 40% of the unskilled minimum wage plus the shortfall; wage claims are settled as under the Sindh Minimum Wages Act, with appeal to the Labour Court within 30 days.
A Domestic Workers Welfare Fund is created; domestic workers register with the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution and employers register (renewable every 3 years).

Disputes go to a Dispute Resolution Committee notified by the Labour Department and must be presented within 30 days of the dispute arising; appeal to the district Appellate Authority within 30 days of the award.
key_provisions.note: Exact places: s.21(3) proviso - dispute presented within 30 days from the date it arises; s.21(4) - appeal within 30 days of the date the award was made; s.22(1) - the Department appoints an Appellate Authority in each district (re-read 2026-10-17).

key_provisions.point: Employer contraventions are fined up to 25% of the unskilled minimum wage (first offence) or 40% (repeat); knowingly employing a child in breach of s.3 is fined 1 to 2 times the unskilled minimum wage.
A household may be inspected only after a complaint and on the Dispute Resolution Committee's direction.

caveats: New law (published June 2026). Dispute Resolution Committees, Inspectors and rules may not be notified yet - confirm the current office with the Sindh Labour Department before naming one.

laws.title: Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017
laws.replaces: Employment of Children Act, 1991, in its application to Sindh (s.24).
laws.scope: Any industrial, commercial or agricultural establishment, mine, business, trade or workplace where economic activity is carried on, including charitable and welfare organisations.

key_provisions.point: A child is a person under 14; an adolescent is a person aged 14 to under 18.
No child may be employed or permitted to work in any establishment.

No adolescent may be employed in hazardous work listed in the Schedule (38 items, including transport, mines and quarries, power-driven cutting machinery, tanning, toxic chemicals, LPG/CNG filling sites, glass furnaces, carpet weaving, stone crushing, lifting 15 kg or more, work at 2 metres height or more, scavenging, building and construction).
Adolescents may work at most 3 hours before a 1-hour rest, 7 hours a day including rest, never between 7 pm and 8 am, never overtime, and not in two establishments on the same day.
Every adolescent worker gets one whole day off each week.
The adolescent hours and notice rules (ss.7-9) do not apply where work is done by the occupier with family help, or in Government-recognised skill schools.

Employing a child: imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs 50,000, or both. In hazardous work: imprisonment up to 3 years and fine of Rs 10,000 to 100,000. In slavery, trafficking, debt bondage, forced labour, sexual exploitation or drug trade: imprisonment of 5 to 10 years and fine of Rs 200,000 to 1,000,000.
Employing an adolescent in hazardous work: imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs 75,000, or both.
Any person, police officer or Labour Inspector may file a complaint; offences are tried by the Labour Court.
The occupier must ensure that working adolescents under 16 (and children acquiring skills) attend compulsory schooling, and keep proof of it.

caveats: For work inside households, the Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 sets a higher minimum age of 16 (see sindh-domestic-workers-welfare-2025, s.3).

laws.title: Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022)
laws.scope: Workplaces across Pakistan; Ombudspersons at federal and provincial level.

amendments.title: Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace (Amendment) Act, 2022
amendments.summary: Incorporated in the Sindh Judicial Academy updated text that was read: 'any person' can complain, wider definitions of employee, employer, harassment (incl. gender discrimination and cyber stalking) and workplace, 90-day decision limit.

key_provisions.point: Extends to the whole of Pakistan.
'Complainant' means any person aggrieved by harassment, including a former employee who was removed, dismissed or resigned, and a parent or guardian where the complainant is a minor.

'Employee' includes regular, contractual, piece-rate, gig, temporary, part-time and freelance workers, and students, performers, artists, sportspersons, interns, trainees, domestic workers, home-based workers and apprentices - paid or unpaid.

'Harassment' means (i) unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favours, stalking or cyber stalking, or other verbal, visual, written or physical conduct of a sexual nature or sexually demeaning attitudes (including gestures) that interfere with work or create an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment, or punishing a refusal or making it a condition of employment; or (ii) discrimination on the basis of gender, whether or not sexual in nature.

'Workplace' covers any place where work or services are performed - including educational institutions, gigs, studios, performance venues, courts, highways and sports facilities - and any situation linked to work outside the office.
Every organisation must constitute a 3-member Inquiry Committee with at least one woman member.
Within 3 days of a written complaint, the Inquiry Committee must send the charges to the accused, who has 7 days to submit a written defence (otherwise the inquiry proceeds ex parte).

Inquiry evidence is confidential; both parties may be accompanied by a CBA representative, friend or colleague; no adverse action may be taken against the complainant or witnesses; the employer or accused must not create a hostile environment for the complainant.

Findings are due within 30 days. Penalties: minor (censure, withholding promotion or increment, stopping at efficiency bar, recovering compensation from the accused) or major (demotion, compulsory retirement, removal, dismissal, suspension or cancellation of a professional licence, fine - part of which may go to the complainant).
A party aggrieved by the Competent Authority's decision may appeal to the Ombudsperson within 30 days.
Ombudspersons are appointed at both the federal and provincial levels.
The complainant may choose to complain either to the Ombudsperson or to the organisation's Inquiry Committee.
The Ombudsperson issues a show-cause notice within 3 days of receiving the complaint; the accused must reply within 5 days.
The Ombudsperson must decide a complaint or appeal within 90 days.
A representation against the Ombudsperson's decision lies to the President (federal) or the Governor (provincial) within 30 days, to be decided within 90 days.
The Ombudsperson has civil-court powers (summons, evidence, inspection of premises, contempt) and can impose the penalties listed in s.4(4).

Employers must adopt the Code of Conduct, form the Inquiry Committee, designate a Competent Authority and display the Code in English and the language of most employees. If they fail, any employee can petition the District Court; the fine is Rs 25,000 to 100,000.

A single incident that makes a person uncomfortable or afraid can be harassment; retaliation (including counter-blast defamation suits) is part of harassment; a delay in reporting does not affect the merits of the case.
FOSPAH's regional offices decide workplace harassment complaints from federal or trans-provincial organisations operating in their region; provincial matters go to the provincial Ombudsperson.

caveats: Text read is the federal Act as amended up to 25 January 2022, compiled by the Sindh Judicial Academy. The Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 refers to it as the 'Sindh Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (Act No. IV of 2010)'. Whether every 2022 amendment is applied identically by the Sindh provincial Ombudsperson was not confirmed - check with that office before asserting it.
Criminal action is separate and possible at the same time: see ppc-509 and, for online conduct, peca-2016.

laws.title: Establishment of the Office of Ombudsman for the Province of Sindh Act, 1991
laws.scope: Complaints of maladministration by Sindh Government agencies.

key_provisions.point: The Provincial Ombudsman (Mohtasib) Sindh investigates complaints of maladministration - decisions contrary to law, arbitrary, biased or discriminatory acts, corruption or favouritism, neglect, delay or inefficiency - by Sindh Government departments and institutions.
Complaints may be made in English, Urdu or Sindhi - online, by email, by post or in person. First approach the agency's higher authorities, and attach that correspondence and a copy of the CNIC.
The Ombudsman's services are free; anonymous complaints are not investigated.

A complaint must be made within 3 months from the day the aggrieved person first had notice of the matter complained of. The Ombudsman may still take up a late complaint if there are special circumstances.
key_provisions.note: Section number and wording from the 1991 Ordinance that preceded the Act; the Ombudsman's official flyer states the same 3-month limit.

key_provisions.point: A person aggrieved by a decision or order of the Ombudsman may make a representation to the Governor of Sindh within 30 days of the decision or order. Count the 30 days from the date of the decision: the statutory wording runs from the decision, while the Ombudsman's FAQ says 30 days from receipt.
key_provisions.note: Section number and wording from the 1991 Ordinance that preceded the Act; the Act's own text could not be opened.

laws.title: Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979
laws.scope: Rented premises (buildings or land, not hotels) in urban areas of Sindh, except premises owned or requisitioned by the Federal or Provincial Government.

amendments.title: Amendments incorporated in the compiled text
amendments.act_number: Sind Ordinances II and XII of 1980, IV of 1984; Sind Act I of 1986; Sindh Ordinance XIV of 2001
amendments.summary: Footnotes in the Sindh Judicial Academy compilation show these amendments; the compiled text was read.

key_provisions.point: 'Landlord' includes anyone entitled to receive the rent; 'tenant' includes a person still in possession after the tenancy ends and heirs in possession; 'premises' means a building or land let on rent, excluding hotels; 'personal use' means use by the owner or the owner's spouse, son or daughter.

Applies to all premises in urban areas (within a Town Committee, Municipal Committee, Municipal Corporation or Metropolitan Corporation) except premises owned or requisitioned by the Federal or Provincial Government; Government may exclude premises or areas by notification.
Rent Controllers - judicial officers with at least 3 years as Civil Judge - are appointed for each district.

Every tenancy agreement must be in writing; if it is not compulsorily registrable, it must be attested by the Rent Controller, a Civil Judge or a First Class Magistrate. The registered or attested deed is the accepted proof of the landlord-tenant relationship.
A landlord cannot charge more than the agreed rent, or more than the fair rent once the Controller has fixed it.

On application by the tenant or the landlord, the Controller fixes the fair rent, considering rents of similar nearby premises, rising construction and repair costs, new taxes, and the annual value used for property tax.
Once fair rent is fixed, it cannot be increased for 3 years; an increase may not exceed 10% per year of the existing rent.

Unless agreed otherwise, rent is due by the 10th of the following month; the landlord must give a written receipt. If the landlord refuses or avoids taking rent, the tenant may send it by postal money order or deposit it with the Rent Controller - these receipts are proof of payment.

A landlord may not cut off electricity, gas, water or similar services without the tenant's consent, an authority's requisition or the Controller's direction. The tenant can apply to the Controller for restoration, and the landlord is punishable with simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both.
If the landlord fails to carry out necessary repairs or whitewashing, the Controller may allow the tenant to do it and deduct the cost from the rent.
No tenant can be evicted except in accordance with this Ordinance.

A landlord who is a widow, a minor whose parents are both dead, a salaried employee retiring within 6 months or already retired, or a person who is (or within 6 months will be) 60, may demand vacant possession for personal use by written notice of at least 2 months. This is not available if the building was let after retirement, turning 60 or being widowed or orphaned, or if the landlord already occupies a building they own. The Controller then orders eviction summarily.

The Controller orders eviction only if satisfied that: the tenant did not pay rent within 15 days after the agreed due date, or within 60 days of it falling due if there is no agreement (a first default of up to 6 months, admitted at the first hearing, can be cured by paying); without written consent the tenant sublet or handed over possession, changed the use, or breached the tenancy conditions; the tenant impaired the value or utility of the premises; the tenant caused nuisance to neighbours; the landlord has sanction to reconstruct; or the landlord genuinely needs it for own use or the use of spouse or children.

If a landlord who obtained possession for reconstruction does not demolish within 6 months or start building within 2 years, or re-lets or does not personally use premises taken for personal use within a year, the evicted tenant can apply to be restored; misuse of a personal-use eviction is fined up to one year's rent.

Once an eviction case is filed, the Controller may order the tenant to deposit arrears and then monthly rent by the 10th of each month; if the tenant fails, the defence is struck off and possession is ordered.
If an eviction application is frivolous or vexatious, the Controller may order the landlord to pay the tenant compensation of up to 10 times the monthly rent.

When ownership changes, the new owner must inform the tenant in writing by registered post; the tenant is not in default if the rent is paid within 30 days of when that notice would normally have arrived.
A respondent gets up to 15 days from the notice to file a written reply; evidence is given by affidavit with cross-examination.
An appeal against a final (not interim) order of the Controller lies to the District Judge within 30 days; the appellate order is final.
Final orders are executed by the Controller, not through a separate suit.
Courts take cognizance of offences under the Ordinance only on the Controller's written complaint.

caveats: First check the location: cantonment areas are governed by the Cantonments Rent Restriction Act, 1963 (see cantonments-rent-restriction-1963); Islamabad by the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001.
Workers living in employer-provided housing: see Standing Order 22 (sindh-standing-orders-2015).
Security deposit refunds are not dealt with in this compiled text (s.6 was omitted in 1984) - refer the user to SLACC rather than inventing a rule.
